messages:
Maria G: Quick sync — proposing we call the new short-lived tokens "microgrants". Purpose: replace most service-to-service long-lived API keys for internal-only calls and narrow resource scoping. Thoughts?
Dan H: +1 on name, sounds clear. Main concern is issuer scale + latency for high-throughput paths.
Olivia P: If we require an auth call to mint per-request tokens that could add 2-20ms depending on cache. We need figures.
Kevin L: Can we avoid a synchronous mint for every request? pattern: cache microgrant in sidecar for prefix matches, TTL = 10s. That keeps lower churn.
Maria G: That's what I had in mind — short TTLs, audience-bound, and audience contains resource path + minimal privileges. Sidecars and SDKs can cache.
Dan H: Revocation model? If a service key is compromised we should be able to invalidate outstanding microgrants. Do we plan revocation lists or a revocation epoch in issuer?
Olivia P: Revocation epoch + per-token "issued_at" tied to current epoch. When we rotate/disable, bump epoch and refuse tokens issued before new epoch. Cheap to check.
Kevin L: Audit volume will spike (issuance events). We need to ensure observability storage handles it. Maybe sample issuance logs and emit full logs on anomalous patterns.
Maria G: Agreed on sampling. Also, we should attach metadata to each microgrant: origin service id, request id, and optional trace_id for debugging.
Dan H: Token format discussion: compact JWT vs opaque reference. Opaque gives more control (server-side checks) but needs a token lookup that hurts latency. JWT avoids lookups but makes revocation harder.
Olivia P: Propose hybrid: signed compact token including issuer, audience, issued_at, ttl, and a short random nonce. Verification typical path: verify signature + epoch check. For forced revocation, issuer can maintain a small blacklist for high-risk nonces only.
Kevin L: How big can token size be? Some downstream infra (gRPC metadata) has limits. Keep token <1600 bytes ideally. Signed compact JWT fits.
Maria G: Perf tradeoffs: verifying signature every hop is CPU-heavy if done in all services. We should offer two modes: lightweight verification in sidecar (cached public key, rotate keys infrequently) and full verification in central gateways.
Dan H: Sidecar approach also helps with rollout — we can centralize heavy checks in gateways for external requests and let internal hops use cached verification.
Olivia P: Operational concerns: key rotation, key discovery, and distribution. We'll piggyback on our existing KMS + config push. Plan: issuer rotates keys weekly, publishes kids, sidecars refresh every minute.
Kevin L: Any changes to RBAC model? Microgrants should reference existing role IDs, not inline permissions. Keeps policies centralized.
Maria G: Yes — microgrant = (principal, role_id, resource_audience, ttl, nonce). Issuer enforces role->permission mapping.
Dan H: Backward compatibility: we'll need a compatibility shim so services still accept legacy project-scoped API keys for a deprecation window. Also detect dance where old keys are used from outside allowed paths.
Olivia P: UX: SDKs should provide an adapter that automatically mints microgrant and refreshes cached token; app code just calls get_token() or uses middleware. Minimal code changes.
Kevin L: Can we prototype with 1) autoscaler metadata service path and 2) internal metrics ingestion? low-risk, measurable traffic.
Maria G: Good candidates. Let's run a 2-week pilot on metrics-ingest, measure latency, mint rate, cache hit ratio, and audit log growth.
Dan H: Action items: Maria to draft mini-RFC with token format + epoch revocation plan; Olivia to sketch SDK flow + caching TTL options; Kevin to prepare sidecar cache design and throughput numbers.
Maria G: I'll create the RFC and set the pilot timeline. Everyone OK with owner assignments?
Olivia P: ACK.
Kevin L: ACK.
Dan H: ACK.
security-bot: Runbook link: <https://intranet.redwood/ops/runbooks/microgrants>. Reminder: follow incident reporting if pilot impacts auth latencies.
